review.value:
**Title:** COREY: A Runtime Scheduling Diagnostic for Selective Scan Kernels

**Synopsis of the paper**

COREY investigates whether fixed-bin activation entropy can select Mamba-1.x selective-scan chunk sizes at runtime, avoiding offline tuning. It combines kernel microbenchmarks, an inline entropy hook, a patched routed kernel, mixed-workload timing, and output-equivalence checks. The principal empirical result is negative: entropy-guided variants preserve tested outputs but remain slower than a tuned static chunk, while sequence length captures the limited workload adaptation observed.

**Summary of Review**

The routed ablation provides useful evidence that online histogram cost outweighs decision value on the measured checkpoint workloads. However, the headline kernel gains are reproduced entirely by the Static-512 baseline: COREY selects the same chunk and has the same latency, so these results establish chunk sensitivity rather than a benefit from entropy. No experiment shows that entropy predicts a changing per-call oracle, and the defined scheduler is inconsistent with the central end-to-end experiment. The claimed bin-count invariance is also contradicted by Table 1. The validated contribution is consequently narrower: an output-preserving runtime diagnostic and a negative characterization for the tested Mamba-1.x settings.

**Strengths**

- The end-to-end experimental design exposes actual runtime costs rather than extrapolating scheduler utility from microbenchmarks. Table 7 routes through a patched live scan kernel and includes fixed chunks, entropy variants, proxies, random routing, a guarded policy, and a learned table, allowing decision cost to be separated from the selected chunk’s performance.

- The mixed-workload analysis identifies a simpler alternative to activation-dependent routing. Section 5.3 finds that sequence length reproduces the per-regime chunk choices for the constructed mixture, helping delimit a regime in which online activation statistics provide no additional decision value.

- The quality evaluation directly compares passive and routed inference. Table 9 reports identical greedy generations and zero task-metric deltas across the tested prompts, supporting the interpretation that the measured latency differences arise from scheduling rather than altered token trajectories.

**Weaknesses**

- The headline kernel gains are not attributable to entropy scheduling. The abstract reports 4.41$\times$ and 3.55$\times$ lower latency than Static-64, but Tables 2 and 5 show that COREY-default and Static-512 use the same chunk and have identical latency and speedup on the consumer and server-class GPUs. The entire reported gain is therefore reproduced by a static configuration that incurs no runtime-statistic cost.

- No experiment establishes that activation entropy predicts a changing per-call optimal chunk. Table 3 reports entropy-selected chunks without a per-distribution static sweep, while Section 5.2 states that all 80 prompts map to one coarse bucket and all sampled layers map to one calibrated chunk. The evaluation consequently measures the cost of the heuristic but provides no evidence that activation values contain useful scheduling information beyond shape or sequence length.

- The scheduler evaluated end to end is inconsistent with the defined method. Equation (2) clips outputs at $C\_{\max}=512$, whereas Table 7 reports entropy and proxy policies routing to chunks 1024 and 2048, despite Section 5.2 stating that entropy is mapped through Eq. (2). This prevents the central routed experiment from being unambiguously interpreted as an evaluation of the specified COREY algorithm.

- The claimed histogram-resolution invariance is contradicted by the paper’s own table. In Table 1, standard-normal $H/\log K$ changes from 0.763 to 0.881 as $K$ increases, while the chunk remains 512 because every calibrated point falls in the same saturated output bucket. Thus, the table demonstrates decision saturation for these examples, not invariance of the entropy signal or robustness near a chunk boundary.

- The related-work positioning omits the closest published chunkwise-kernel analysis. Tiled Flash Linear Attention derives runtime-optimal chunks from architectural dimensions and accelerator arithmetic intensity (Beck et al., 2025), while Section 2 attributes Flash Linear Attention to Dao and Gu rather than the published GLA work (Yang et al., 2024). These results bear directly on whether chunk choice is primarily hardware- and shape-driven rather than activation-driven.

- The static-oracle and transfer claims exceed the evaluation’s resolution and coverage. In Table 7, Static-512 leads Static-128 by 1.20 ms against standard deviations of 10.17 and 12.11 ms; Table 8’s comparable rows span only 0.4 ms without uncertainty; and Table 5’s TPU and Tesla entries contain no sweep. These data support near-equivalence in the tested settings, but not a unique or cross-platform oracle.

**Suggestions for Improvement**

- Organize the evidence in causal order: static chunk sensitivity, variation in the per-call oracle, feature-to-oracle prediction, routed decision cost, and output preservation. The current fusion prototype and Hadamard discussion interrupt this progression without materially supporting the routed scheduler.

- Add a system-path schematic before the experiments. Sections 5.1–5.2 alternate among isolated Triton timing, a Python-dispatch harness, a passive hook, and a patched live kernel; showing where entropy collection, synchronization, dispatch, and scan execution occur would clarify which costs each table includes.

- Quantify the amortization trade-off between one-time static profiling and recurring online scheduling. Reporting profiling cost, expected request volume, and break-even behavior would place the proposed replacement for offline tuning on an operationally meaningful scale.

- Develop the staged policy proposed in Section 5.3 as the forward-looking systems hypothesis. A low-cost shape or length gate could reserve activation-dependent analysis for regions where competing static chunks have demonstrably different regret.

**Additional Details and Minor Issues**

- Equation (1) with $\epsilon>0$ does not yield the exact stated range $H\_e\in[0,1]$ or exact uniform entropy $\log K$.

- Table 2 combines direct-Triton latency with speedup from a separate dispatch harness, so the displayed latency ratio differs from the displayed speedup.

- Theorem 2’s strictness condition is incomplete: a non-permutation doubly stochastic matrix can preserve a nonuniform vector by mixing coordinates with equal probabilities.

- Section 5.3 describes 160 prompts with 20 per regime, whereas Table 8 reports eight samples per regime.

- Table 9 establishes identical generated tokens, but not bitwise equality of hidden states or logits; the “recurrence-preserving” interpretation should be scoped accordingly.

**References**

Beck, M., Pöppel, K., Lippe, P., & Hochreiter, S. (2025). Tiled Flash Linear Attention: More efficient linear RNN and xLSTM kernels. *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 38*. ([proceedings.neurips.cc](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/6cb81234ab47027e991728ed7dd76735-Abstract-Conference.html))

Yang, S., Wang, B., Shen, Y., Panda, R., & Kim, Y. (2024). Gated linear attention transformers with hardware-efficient training. In *Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning* (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, Vol. 235, pp. 56501–56523). ([proceedings.mlr.press](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/yang24ab.html))

title.value: This paper studies runtime chunk-size scheduling for Mamba selective scan kernels using activation entropy as an adaptive signal. While the paper addresses an important systems problem and provides extensive experimental analysis, the proposed entropy-based scheduler does not demonstrate practical advantages over carefully tuned static scheduling. The main experimental findings show that the static oracle remains superior in realistic end-to-end inference settings, limiting the significance of the proposed approach.

review.value:
This paper presents COREY, a runtime scheduling framework for optimizing selective scan kernels in Mamba-based state space models (SSMs). The paper focuses on the challenge that selective scan performance is highly sensitive to scheduling decisions, particularly chunk size selection, while conventional approaches rely on offline profiling for specific model, hardware, and workload combinations.

The authors propose using activation entropy as a runtime signal for dynamically selecting scan chunk sizes. COREY estimates fixed-bin Shannon entropy from intermediate activation tensors and normalizes the entropy value to derive a chunk selection rule. The proposed scheduler is integrated into the Mamba inference pipeline through a runtime hook, where activation statistics are collected during execution and used to determine the chunk size passed to the selective scan kernel.

The paper evaluates COREY through multiple levels of experiments, including a synthetic prototype cost model, kernel-level benchmarks across different hardware platforms, and end-to-end inference experiments using real Mamba checkpoints. The authors further evaluate several scheduling variants, including guarded routing and lightweight learned-table approaches, to analyze the trade-off between adaptation capability and scheduling overhead.

The reported results show that COREY can reproduce offline-selected chunk configurations in some kernel-level benchmark scenarios. However, the end-to-end experiments indicate that entropy-guided scheduling does not outperform the best static chunk configuration and introduces additional runtime overhead. The authors conclude that activation entropy is a feasible diagnostic signal for selective scan scheduling, but current entropy-based runtime adaptation does not provide a consistent throughput advantage over carefully tuned static scheduling.

strengths.value:
1. The paper addresses a relevant systems problem
The paper studies runtime scheduling for Mamba selective scan kernels, where chunk-size selection can affect kernel efficiency.
2. The paper attempts to provide an empirical analysis of runtime scheduling limitations
The paper evaluates COREY through multiple experimental settings, including kernel-level benchmarks and end-to-end inference measurements.

weaknesses.value:
1. The main contribution is not supported by the final experimental results. 
The central motivation of the paper is that activation entropy can replace offline profiling for runtime chunk-size selection. However, the experimental results do not demonstrate this advantage.
In the end-to-end evaluation, the authors report that entropy-guided variants do not outperform the best static chunk configuration. The guarded scheduler and learned-table variants reduce some scheduling overhead, but they remain slower than the static oracle.
This creates a fundamental issue: the proposed method demonstrates that runtime entropy-based scheduling is possible, but it does not demonstrate that such adaptation is beneficial in realistic inference scenarios.
2. The relationship between activation entropy and optimal chunk size is insufficiently justified.
The paper assumes that activation entropy provides meaningful information for predicting kernel scheduling decisions. However, the connection between entropy and optimal chunk size is not sufficiently established.
Chunk-size selection is primarily influenced by GPU-specific factors such as register pressure, shared memory usage, occupancy, memory access patterns, and kernel launch overhead.
The paper provides an entropy-to-chunk mapping function, but it does not explain why entropy should reliably capture these hardware-level optimization factors.
The current experiments mainly show that certain activation distributions map to the same chunk size as offline profiling. This does not establish that entropy provides information beyond simpler features such as sequence length, layer index, tensor shape, or hardware profiling.
3. The reported speedups rely on weak baseline comparisons.
The paper highlights significant kernel-level speedups, such as the reported $4.41\times$ improvement. However, these improvements are mainly measured against Static-64.
The paper itself shows that Static-512 is the optimal static configuration in these settings. Therefore, the reported speedup largely reflects comparison against a non-optimal baseline rather than an improvement introduced by COREY.
The more meaningful comparison is between COREY and the best static oracle. Under this comparison, COREY does not provide a performance improvement.
4. The evaluation does not sufficiently demonstrate workload diversity.
The motivation of runtime adaptation is to handle diverse and changing workloads. However, the evaluation does not sufficiently explore workload variation.
For example, the LongBench evaluation shows that prompt-level entropy distributions are relatively concentrated, and most inputs select similar chunk configurations. This raises questions about whether runtime adaptation is necessary in practical scenarios.
Additional evaluation across different model architectures, batch sizes, sequence length distributions, serving workloads, and GPU platforms would be necessary.
5. The experimental methodology contains inconsistencies across sections.
The paper uses different entropy calibration settings throughout the experiments, including $H_{ref}=8.0$ and $H_{ref}=\log K$. Although the authors explain that earlier settings are sensitivity analyses, some reported results rely on configurations that are not the final default method.
Furthermore, the paper mixes isolated kernel latency measurements with end-to-end inference latency measurements. A clearer separation between microbenchmark results and deployment-level performance would improve the evaluation.
6. The paper lacks sufficient visualization of the proposed mechanism.
The proposed contribution relies heavily on the relationship:
\[
\text{activation entropy}
\rightarrow
\text{chunk selection}
\rightarrow
\text{kernel performance}.
\]
However, the paper provides limited visualization of this process. There are no clear figures showing entropy distributions across workloads, entropy-to-chunk decision boundaries, correlation between entropy values and optimal chunk sizes, or latency trade-offs across scheduling choices.
For a runtime scheduling framework, such visual analysis is important to understand whether the proposed signal captures meaningful workload characteristics.

justification.value:
The paper investigates an interesting systems problem and provides considerable engineering effort with extensive experiments. However, the main weakness is that the proposed runtime scheduler does not demonstrate practical improvement over strong static scheduling baselines.

The key motivation of replacing offline profiling with activation entropy-based adaptation is not validated by the experimental results. The strongest reported improvements come from comparisons against suboptimal static configurations, while comparisons against the actual static oracle show that COREY introduces overhead without improving throughput.

A stronger paper would need to demonstrate that activation entropy provides unique predictive information for chunk-size optimization and leads to measurable deployment-level improvements over competitive static tuning approaches.

feedback.value:
The paper claims that activation entropy can replace offline profiling. Given that Static-512 consistently outperforms COREY in end-to-end experiments, what practical deployment scenario benefits from COREY?

Can the authors provide evidence that activation entropy provides useful scheduling information beyond simpler features such as sequence length, layer index, tensor dimensions, or offline profiling?
    
What is the theoretical justification for the relationship between activation entropy and optimal chunk size? Is this relationship causal or only empirical correlation?
    
The reported kernel-level speedups are mainly relative to Static-64. Can the authors clarify COREY's improvement compared with the strongest static tuning baseline under identical conditions?
    
Since LongBench prompts show narrow entropy distributions and similar chunk selections, what motivates per-request runtime adaptation in realistic serving workloads?

title.value: Review of the paper "COREY: A Runtime Scheduling Diagnostic for Selective Scan Kernels"

review.value: The paper proposes COREY, an entropy-based runtime scheduler for selecting Mamba-1 selective scan kernel chunk sizes. While the paper demonstrates wins over a (somewhat arbitrary) Static-64 baseline, the end-to-end results are slower than the best static configuration. The paper's most defensible conclusion is therefore a negative one -- online entropy-based chunk size selection does not justify its overhead on the evaluated workload.

strengths.value:
- Clear and transparent presentation of negative results
- Measures real runtime overhead

weaknesses.value:
- No meaningful positive end-to-end result
- Headline speedup numbers are over a weak baseline
- No batching is discussed, which hampers real-world usefulness
- Not enough evaluations on the broader family of linear attention architectures

justification.value: Overall, the submission is pretty weak. I appreciate the authors for transparently disclosing that COREY loses end-to-end. The takeaway is that a hand-calibrated rule selects the same chunk size as a static offline oracle, whereas the actual system incurs a slowdown. (The headline 4.41x number compares against chunk size 64, while COREY's calibrated rule simply picks static chunk size 512.) While I generally agree that publications regarding failed results should be encouraged in the scientific community, this paper, as it stands, does not offer enough useful insights. Further, it does not seem to work with batching, a de facto approach in real-world inference. It's also not evaluated on modern linear attention architectures like Mamba2, Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, etc.

feedback.value: As it stands, I think the paper should go through a major revamp to be framed as a clear, concise negative-results study with batched serving experiments, comparisons to standard auto-tuning baselines (if any), evaluations across more model architectures, etc. In its current form, it doesn't demonstrate that entropy-guided runtime scheduling improves inference performance or offers a sufficiently general insight/pointer to a direction.

title.value: COREY: A Runtime Scheduling Diagnostic for Selective Scan Kernels

TLDR.value: COREY is a runtime scheduling diagnostic for Mamba-1.x selective-scan kernels: entropy can match a static kernel oracle, but routed inference remains slower than a tuned static chunk due to measurement and dispatch overhead.

abstract.value: Mamba selective state space models (SSMs) offer linear-time sequence modeling but remain sensitive to scan-kernel scheduling choices. We present COREY, a \emph{concept-and-feasibility} runtime scheduler that uses fixed-bin activation entropy as a signal for selecting selective-scan chunk sizes. We evaluate COREY across three tiers: a prototype cost model, a real-checkpoint kernel-timing study, and a routed end-to-end ablation on modern GPU hardware. At the kernel level, the calibrated rule ($H_{\text{ref}}{=}\log K$) selects the locally optimal chunk size and matches a one-time-profile static oracle on the measured consumer and server-class GPU sweeps ($4.41\times$ and $3.55\times$ lower latency than Static-64, respectively); H800 results are reported separately as a legacy-reference sensitivity diagnostic and as the routed end-to-end platform. Routing the selected chunk into a patched live scan kernel closes an engineering gap but does not yield an end-to-end speedup: in a unified routed ablation, the best static chunk outperforms all entropy-guided and proxy-based variants, with sampled-histogram COREY incurring $+4.6\%$ overhead; a guarded fallback policy routes long-context calls to Static-512 and reduces overhead to $+1.3\%$; a lightweight seq-len-keyed learned table reduces it further to $+0.7\%$; both are still slower than the static oracle, which avoids scheduling cost entirely. An 80-prompt LongBench evaluation confirms exact greedy-token agreement and zero metric deltas between passive and routed inference paths. A mixed-regime workload study across diverse prompt types shows that a single sequence-length rule replicates the per-regime optimal chunk oracle for a balanced serving mix, making complex regime-aware adaptation unnecessary. COREY is validated as a quality-preserving runtime scheduling diagnostic; its principal finding is that current activation entropy statistics do not deliver a robust throughput advantage over static chunk tuning on measured SSM checkpoint workloads.
